title: Is Sugar Good for a Hangover? Blood Sugar, Cravings, and What to Eat
excerpt: Does sugar help a hangover? How alcohol lowers blood sugar overnight, why you crave sweets the morning after, which sugary foods help, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Is sugar good for a hangover? How alcohol lowers blood sugar, why you crave sweets, the best sugary foods and drinks, and when shakiness needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a moderate amount of sugar can help a hangover a little, mostly by fixing one specific problem: low blood sugar. Alcohol interferes with your liver's ability to make new glucose, so after a night of drinking, especially if you skipped dinner, your blood sugar can dip lower than usual. That can add to the shakiness, weakness, irritability, and headache you feel the next morning. A glass of juice, a banana, or toast with honey can take the edge off those symptoms. What sugar can't do is fix the rest of a hangover. There is no good evidence that sugar speeds up how fast your body clears alcohol in any way that matters, and a big sugar binge on its own often leads to a crash an hour later.

**The quick rules:** Pair sugar with real food. Some carbs plus protein and fat (eggs on toast, a smoothie with yogurt, oatmeal with fruit) steadies your blood sugar better than candy or soda alone. Drink fluids with a little sugar and salt if you're dehydrated, because a small amount of glucose actually helps your gut absorb sodium and water. Skip the giant soda and donut breakfast, which tends to spike and then drop you. And if you have diabetes or take blood sugar medication, be careful: alcohol can push blood sugar dangerously low for many hours after your last drink.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research for healthy adults who drink socially. It isn't a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **When to see a doctor:** Get medical help if you have diabetes and your blood sugar stays low or keeps dropping after you've eaten, if shakiness, sweating, or confusion don't improve within 15 to 20 minutes of eating something sugary, if you can't keep any food or fluids down for more than a day, or if you notice severe confusion, a seizure, very slow or irregular breathing, or someone who can't be woken up after drinking. Those last signs can mean alcohol poisoning or severe low blood sugar, and you should call 911 right away. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that start a day or more after you stop drinking, especially after several days of heavy drinking, can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which also needs medical care rather than a snack.

## Is Sugar Good for a Hangover? What's Actually Going On

To understand why sugar sometimes helps, you need to know what alcohol does to your blood sugar overnight.

Your body keeps blood glucose steady in two main ways between meals. First, your liver breaks down stored sugar, called glycogen, and releases it into your blood. Second, when those stores run low, your liver builds brand-new glucose from other materials such as lactate and amino acids. That second process is called gluconeogenesis, which simply means "making new sugar."

Alcohol gets in the way of the second process. When your liver breaks down alcohol, it uses up a helper molecule called NAD+ and produces a lot of its partner, NADH. The liver needs NAD+ to make new glucose. With the balance tipped toward NADH, the sugar-making assembly line slows down. This is a well-established piece of liver biochemistry, and it's the reason alcohol-related low blood sugar is described in medical textbooks.

On its own, that usually isn't a big deal. If you ate a decent meal before or while drinking, your glycogen stores carry you through the night. The trouble starts when the two things stack up:

- **You drank on an empty stomach or skipped dinner.** Your glycogen stores were already lower going in.
- **You drank a lot, or late into the night.** Your liver spent hours prioritizing alcohol over glucose production.
- **You slept late and haven't eaten.** By mid-morning, you may have gone 15 hours or more without food.

Put those together and you can wake up with blood sugar on the low side of normal. Low blood sugar has its own set of symptoms: shakiness, sweating, weakness, a racing heart, irritability, trouble concentrating, headache, and hunger. If that list sounds a lot like a hangover, that's the point. Some of what you feel the morning after may be your blood sugar, and that part responds well to food.

## Does Low Blood Sugar Cause Hangovers?

Here's where the popular advice gets ahead of the evidence. Low blood sugar is one piece of the hangover puzzle, but researchers don't think it's the main cause.

Reviews of hangover research, including work from the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have looked at whether blood glucose levels line up with how bad people feel. Studies that measured glucose during hangovers have generally not found it to track closely with hangover severity. Many people with brutal hangovers have blood sugar in the normal range.

The current thinking is that hangovers come from several overlapping causes:

- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, and the levels of inflammatory signaling molecules seem to relate to how bad a hangover feels.
- **Acetaldehyde.** This toxic by-product of alcohol breakdown contributes to nausea, flushing, and a fast heart rate.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster but breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Dehydration and electrolyte shifts.** Alcohol makes you urinate more, though dehydration doesn't explain everything either.
- **Congeners.** These are other compounds in drinks, found in higher amounts in dark liquors like bourbon and red wine.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid.

So the realistic view is this: sugar fixes one possible contributor. If your blood sugar is low, you'll probably feel noticeably better after eating something. If it isn't, sugar won't do much for your headache, nausea, or fatigue beyond the general comfort of eating. For a full rundown of what's behind the misery and what helps each part, see our [complete guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide).

## Why You Crave Sugar When You're Hungover

That powerful urge for pancakes, soda, or candy the morning after is real, and there are a few reasons for it.

1. **Your body is asking for fuel.** If your blood sugar is on the low side, your brain notices fast. Glucose is its main fuel, and low levels trigger hunger, especially for quick carbohydrates.
2. **You're tired.** Poor sleep from drinking raises hunger and shifts appetite toward high-calorie, high-sugar food. Sleep researchers have seen this pattern in studies of sleep restriction in general, not just after drinking.
3. **Comfort and habit.** Many people associate greasy, sweet breakfasts with recovering from a night out. A big part of the craving is simply wanting to feel better quickly.
4. **Dehydration can feel like hunger.** Thirst and hunger signals overlap, so some of the craving may ease after a large glass of water.

None of this means you should fight the craving. It means you should feed it well. A breakfast with carbs, protein, and some fat answers the signal and keeps you level, while a sugar-only fix often brings the craving back within an hour or two.

## The Sugar Crash Problem

Eating a lot of simple sugar on an empty stomach causes a quick rise in blood sugar. Your body responds by releasing insulin to bring it back down. In some people, especially when the meal was mostly sugar with little protein, fat, or fiber, that drop can overshoot and leave you feeling shaky, tired, and hungry again a couple of hours later. Doctors call this reactive hypoglycemia, and it's more noticeable in some people than others.

When you're already hungover, that second dip is the last thing you want. It's why a 20-ounce soda and a glazed donut can feel great for half an hour and terrible afterward. The fix isn't avoiding sugar. It's adding food that slows down how fast the sugar hits your blood:

- **Protein** such as eggs, yogurt, cottage cheese, or a turkey sandwich
- **Fat** such as peanut butter, avocado, or cheese
- **Fiber** such as whole fruit, oats, or whole-grain toast

Eggs are a particularly good partner. They're easy on the stomach and supply protein and cysteine, which we cover in our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).

## The Best Ways to Get Sugar When You're Hungover

If your goal is to steady your blood sugar and feel human again, here are the options that tend to work best, roughly from most to least helpful.

| Option | Why it helps | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Toast with honey or jam plus eggs | Quick carbs for a fast lift, protein to keep you steady | Not much, if you can stomach it |
| Banana | Easy to digest, natural sugar, potassium | Not much on its own for protein |
| Oatmeal with fruit and a little honey | Slow-release carbs with a sweet start | Takes a few minutes to make |
| Fruit smoothie with yogurt | Fluids, sugar, protein, and easy on a queasy stomach | Store-bought versions can be very high in sugar |
| Orange or apple juice (a small glass) | Fast sugar, fluids, and some potassium | Acidic juice can bother an irritated stomach |
| Sports drink or electrolyte drink | Fluids, salt, and a small amount of sugar together | Full-sugar versions add up fast if you drink several |
| Crackers or plain toast | Bland carbs for a sensitive stomach | Little nutritional value beyond carbs |
| Soda, candy, pastries alone | Very quick lift | Crash risk, extra stomach acid from soda, little else |

### Fruit

Fruit is one of the best ways to get sugar when you're hungover. It comes with water, fiber, and minerals like potassium, which you lose more of when you urinate a lot. Bananas are the classic choice because they're bland and easy on the stomach. Watermelon and berries add fluids. Our guide to the [best fruits for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-fruits-for-hangover) compares the main options.

### Honey

Honey shows up in a lot of hangover advice because it's high in fructose, a type of sugar the body handles differently from glucose. Some older lab and small human studies explored whether fructose speeds up alcohol clearance, and the results were mixed and inconsistent. There is no good evidence that a spoonful of honey clears alcohol from your blood faster or prevents a hangover. Honey is still a perfectly fine way to get some quick sugar, especially on toast or stirred into tea or oatmeal. Just treat it as food, not medicine.

### Juice

A small glass of juice is a fast and easy way to raise low blood sugar, and it's what doctors suggest people with diabetes use to treat a low. Orange juice also gives you some vitamin C and potassium. The downside is acidity: if your stomach is burning, apple juice or diluted juice may sit better. Keep it to one glass and pair it with food, because juice is mostly sugar without the fiber of whole fruit.

### Sports drinks and electrolyte drinks

This is where a little sugar does something useful beyond raising blood sugar. Your small intestine absorbs sodium and glucose together through a shared transport system, and water follows. That's the science behind oral rehydration solutions, which use a modest, balanced amount of sugar and salt to help the body take in fluid more efficiently than water alone. If you're dehydrated after drinking, a drink with both salt and some sugar can help you rehydrate. You don't need a huge amount of sugar for this effect. Lower-sugar electrolyte drinks are built around it. Our [Gatorade for hangover guide](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover) and our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) go into the details.

### Soda and candy

These work if your blood sugar is genuinely low and nothing else is available. But they're the most likely to cause a crash, carbonation can worsen nausea and bloating, and cola adds caffeine, which some people tolerate well and others find makes their jitters worse. Use them as a stopgap, then eat a real meal.

## Does Sugar in Your Drinks Make Hangovers Worse?

People often blame sugary cocktails for their worst hangovers. The truth is more complicated.

**Sugary drinks are easy to drink fast.** Sweet mixers hide the taste of alcohol, which makes it easy to drink more than you planned and to drink it quickly. More alcohol is the single biggest driver of a worse hangover. In that sense, sugary cocktails often lead to bad hangovers indirectly.

**Sugar itself isn't a proven hangover cause.** There's no strong evidence that the sugar in a drink, separate from the amount of alcohol, makes hangovers worse. The type of alcohol matters more. Dark liquors and red wine contain more congeners, and some studies have found that drinks high in congeners, like bourbon, produce worse hangovers than clearer spirits like vodka at the same dose.

**Diet mixers may raise your blood alcohol faster.** Here's a twist. A small 2013 study by Cecile Marczinski and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, found that people who drank vodka mixed with a diet soda reached a higher breath alcohol level than when they drank the same amount of vodka mixed with regular soda. The likely reason is that sugar slows how fast the stomach empties into the small intestine, where alcohol is absorbed quickly. It was a small study, so it's not the final word, but it's a useful reminder that switching to diet mixers doesn't make drinking "lighter."

**Cocktails can be very high in sugar.** Margaritas, daiquiris, and punch can contain a lot of sugar per glass. That isn't a hangover issue so much as a calorie and blood-sugar issue, especially if you have diabetes.

The practical takeaway: count drinks, not grams of sugar. Pace yourself, alternate alcohol with water, and choose clearer drinks if you're prone to bad hangovers.

## Should You Eat Sugar Before or While Drinking?

Eating before you drink is one of the most useful things you can do, and carbohydrates are part of that. Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption, so your blood alcohol rises more gently and peaks lower. A full meal also tops up your glycogen stores, which protects you from the overnight blood sugar dip described above.

But the best pre-drinking meal is a balanced one, not a sugary one. A plate with protein, fat, and complex carbohydrates, such as pasta with chicken, a burrito, or salmon with rice, does more than a candy bar. Sugar alone digests fast and won't keep your stomach full for long.

If you're curious what happens when you skip this step, our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why the same number of drinks hits much harder without food.

A late-night snack before bed can also help, especially if you didn't eat much during the evening. Some toast, a banana, or a bowl of cereal gives your body something to work with overnight. Just don't rely on it to undo a heavy night.

## The Hangover Shakes and Low Blood Sugar

Shaky hands the morning after a night of drinking are common. Low blood sugar is one possible cause, which is why eating often helps within 15 to 20 minutes. Other causes include dehydration, poor sleep, caffeine, anxiety, and the nervous system rebounding after being slowed down by alcohol.

Here's a simple test. Eat something with quick sugar and some protein, drink water, and wait 20 minutes. If the shakes ease, low blood sugar was probably part of it. If they don't improve, or they're getting worse over the day, something else is going on. Our [hangover shakes guide](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the other causes in more detail.

Shaking that starts or gets worse a day or more after you stop drinking is different. Especially after several days or weeks of heavy drinking, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. That isn't a sugar problem, and it's a reason to talk to a doctor or go to urgent care.

## If You Have Diabetes: Sugar, Alcohol, and the Next Morning

This is the most important section on this page if it applies to you. For people who take insulin or certain diabetes pills, especially sulfonylureas such as glipizide or glyburide, alcohol can cause low blood sugar that is serious and long lasting.

- **The risk lasts a long time.** Diabetes organizations warn that alcohol can lower blood sugar for many hours after your last drink, including overnight and into the next day.
- **Low blood sugar can look like being drunk.** Confusion, slurred speech, and unsteadiness are signs of both. People around you may assume you're just intoxicated, and you may not recognize it yourself.
- **The usual warning signs can be dulled.** Alcohol and sleep can make it harder to notice a low until it's well underway.

Practical steps that diabetes groups generally recommend include eating when you drink, checking your blood sugar before bed and the next morning, having a snack before bed if your levels are on the low side, wearing medical ID, and making sure someone with you knows what to do. Keep fast sugar, such as glucose tablets or juice, within reach. If you use a continuous glucose monitor, set it to alert you to lows overnight.

Talk to your doctor or diabetes educator about how alcohol fits with your specific medication. Our [alcohol and blood sugar management guide for diabetes](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers this in much more depth.

## A Simple Hangover Morning Plan

If you've woken up feeling rough and you're reaching for something sweet, here's a sensible order:

1. **Drink a large glass of water first.** Then keep sipping through the morning.
2. **Have a small amount of quick sugar if you feel shaky or weak.** Half a glass of juice, a banana, or a spoonful of honey on toast.
3. **Eat a real breakfast within the hour.** Eggs, toast, oatmeal, yogurt, or whatever your stomach can handle. Aim for some protein.
4. **Add salt and fluids if you're dehydrated.** An electrolyte drink, broth, or salty crackers with water.
5. **Rest.** Sleep remains one of the most effective hangover treatments, even if it's not exciting.
6. **Go easy on the extras.** Large amounts of coffee, energy drinks, or more alcohol ("hair of the dog") tend to delay recovery rather than speed it up.

For a bigger list of breakfast and snack ideas, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

## Myths About Sugar and Hangovers

**Myth: Sugar "burns off" alcohol faster.** Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though it varies by person. Some old studies looked at whether fructose speeds this up, with mixed results. There is no good evidence that eating sugar sobers you up or meaningfully shortens a hangover.

**Myth: A hangover is just low blood sugar.** Low blood sugar can be one part, but studies haven't found it to closely match how bad hangovers are. Inflammation, poor sleep, acetaldehyde, and dehydration all play roles.

**Myth: Sugary cocktails cause the worst hangovers because of the sugar.** The amount of alcohol and the type of drink matter far more. Sweet drinks make it easier to drink more, which is the real problem.

**Myth: You should avoid all sugar when hungover.** A moderate amount of sugar, especially from fruit, juice, or alongside a balanced meal, is a sensible part of recovery. It's large amounts of sugar on its own that tend to backfire.

**Myth: Diet mixers are the safer choice.** Diet mixers save calories, but a small study suggests they may lead to a higher blood alcohol level than sugary mixers for the same amount of alcohol.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

Food, fluids, and sleep are the foundation of feeling better after drinking. No supplement replaces them, and no supplement makes heavy drinking safe.

Some people add DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, as part of their routine on nights they drink. Research on DHM has looked at how it affects alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol, but most of that work has been done in animals and lab settings, with limited human data. It's an area of real interest, not a settled answer, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone. It also has nothing to do with blood sugar, so it doesn't replace eating if you feel shaky.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you have diabetes or take regular medication, check with your doctor before adding any supplement.

The most reliable approach is still the simple one: eat before you drink, pace yourself, alternate with water, and follow our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol slows your liver's ability to make new glucose, so blood sugar can dip after drinking, especially if you didn't eat.
- A moderate amount of sugar can ease the shaky, weak, irritable part of a hangover, particularly when you pair it with protein and fat.
- Low blood sugar is only one piece of a hangover. Sugar won't fix inflammation, poor sleep, or nausea, and there's no good evidence it speeds up alcohol clearance.
- Fruit, a small glass of juice, honey on toast, and electrolyte drinks with a bit of sugar and salt are better choices than soda and candy alone.
- If you have diabetes, alcohol can cause dangerous lows for many hours. Check your levels, keep fast sugar nearby, and talk to your doctor.
- If shakiness or confusion doesn't improve after eating, or you see signs of alcohol poisoning or withdrawal, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is sugar good for a hangover?**

In moderation, yes. Alcohol interferes with your liver's ability to make new glucose, so your blood sugar can run low the morning after, especially if you skipped dinner. A little sugar from fruit, juice, or honey on toast can ease shakiness, weakness, and irritability. It works best alongside protein and fat. Sugar won't fix the other causes of a hangover, such as inflammation, poor sleep, and nausea.

**Why do I crave sugar when I'm hungover?**

There are a few reasons. Your blood sugar may be on the low side because alcohol slows glucose production in the liver. Poor sleep after drinking also increases hunger and the urge for high-calorie foods. Dehydration can feel like hunger too. A balanced breakfast with some quick carbs and protein usually answers the craving better than sugar alone.

**Does sugar help you sober up faster?**

No. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink per hour on average. Some older studies tested whether fructose, the sugar in fruit and honey, speeds this up, but the results were mixed. There is no good evidence that eating sugar sobers you up or lowers your blood alcohol in any meaningful way.

**Is honey good for a hangover?**

Honey is a fine source of quick sugar, and it's easy to add to toast, tea, or oatmeal. It's often promoted because of its fructose content, but there is no good evidence that honey clears alcohol faster or prevents hangovers. Treat it as a pleasant way to get some sugar, not as a cure.

**Do sugary drinks make hangovers worse?**

Not directly, as far as current research shows. Sweet mixers make it easy to drink more alcohol, and to drink it faster, and more alcohol is what makes hangovers worse. The type of drink matters too: dark liquors and red wine contain more congeners, which have been linked to worse hangovers. Interestingly, one small study found diet mixers led to higher breath alcohol levels than regular mixers.

**Should I drink soda for a hangover?**

A small amount of regular soda can help if your blood sugar is low and nothing else is available. But soda on its own tends to cause a sugar crash, carbonation can make nausea and bloating worse, and cola adds caffeine. Water, an electrolyte drink, or a small glass of juice plus some food is usually a better choice.

**Can low blood sugar from drinking be dangerous?**

For most healthy social drinkers, the dip is mild and improves after eating. It can be serious for people with diabetes who take insulin or certain diabetes pills, for anyone who drank heavily without eating for a long time, and for children who accidentally drink alcohol. If shaking, sweating, or confusion doesn't improve within 15 to 20 minutes of eating sugar, or someone is very confused or hard to wake, get medical help right away.

**What should I eat for a hangover instead of just sugar?**

Combine quick carbs with protein and some fat. Good examples include eggs on toast, oatmeal with banana, yogurt with fruit and honey, or a smoothie made with yogurt. Add fluids and some salt, such as an electrolyte drink or broth, if you're dehydrated. This keeps your blood sugar steady instead of spiking and dropping.
